source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ ἡδονῇ καὶ ἐπιθυμίᾳ ὑποπίπτειν γάμος δοκεῖ, καὶ περὶ τούτου διαληπτέον. γάμος μὲν οὖν ἐστι σύνοδος ἀνδρὸς καὶ γυναικὸς ἡ πρώτη κατὰ νόμον ἐπὶ γνησίων τέκνων σπορᾷ. ὁ γοῦν κωμικὸς Μένανδρος παίδων (φησὶν) ἐπ’ ἀρότῳ γνησίων δίδωμί σοί γε τὴν ἐμαυτοῦ θυγατέρα. ζητοῦμεν δὲ εἰ γαμητέον, ὅπερ τῶν κατὰ τὸ πρός τί πως ἔχειν ὠνομασμένων ἐστίν. τίνι γὰρ γαμητέον ὅπερ καὶ πῶς ἔχοντι, καὶ τίνα καὶ πῶς ἔχουσαν; οὔτε γὰρ παντὶ γαμητέον οὔτε πάντοτε, ἀλλὰ καὶ κρόνος ἐστὶν ἐν ᾧ καθήκει, καὶ πρόσωπον ᾧ προσήκει, καὶ ἡλικία μέχρι τίνος. οὔτε οὖν παντὶ γαμητέον πᾶσαν οὔτε πάντοτε, ἀλλ’ οὐδὲ παντελῶς καὶ ἀνέδην, ἀλλὰ τῷ πως ἔχοντι καὶ ὁποίαν καὶ ὁπότε δεῖ, καὶ χάριν παίδων καὶ κατὰ πάντα ὁμοίαν καὶ μὴ βίᾳ ἢ ἀνάγκῃ στέργουσαν τὸν ἀγαπῶντα ἄνδρα. ὅθεν ὁ Ἀβραάμ φησιν ἐπὶ τῆς γυναικὸς σκηπτόμενος ὡς ἀδελφῆς· ἀδελφή μοί ἐστιν ἐκ πατρός, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐκ μητρός, ἐγένετο δέ μοι καὶ εἰς γυναῖκα, τὰς ὁμομητρίους μὴ δεῖν ἄγεσθαι πρὸς γάμον διδάσκων. Ἐπίωμεν δὲ ἐν βραχεῖ τὴν ἱστορίαν. Πλάτων μὲν ἐν τοῖς ἐκτὸς ἀγαθοῖς τάττει τὸν γάμον, ἐπισκευάσας τὴν ἀθανασίαν τοῦ γένους ἡμῶν καὶ οἱονεὶ διαμονήν τινα παισὶ παίδων μεταλαμπαδευομένην. Δημόκριτος δὲ γάμον καὶ παιδοποιίαν παραιτεῖται διὰ τὰς πολλὰς ἐξ αὐτῶν ἀηδίας τε καὶ ἀφολκὰς ἀπὸ τῶν ἀναγκαιοτέρων. συγκατατάττεται δὲ αὐτῷ καὶ Ἐπίκουρος καὶ ὅσοι ἐν ἡδονῇ καὶ ἀοχλησίᾳ, ἔτι δὲ καὶ ἀλυπίᾳ τἀγαθὸν τίθενται. ἔτι κατὰ μὲν τοὺς ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς ἀδιάφορον ὅ τε γάμος ἥ τε παιδοτροφία, κατὰ δὲ τοὺς ἐκ τοῦ Περιπάτου ἀγαθόν. συλλήβδην οὗτοι μέχρι γλώττης ἀγαγόντες τὰ δόγματα ἡδοναῖς ἐδουλώθησαν. οἳ μὲν παλλακίσιν, οἳ δὲ ἑταίραις μειρακίοις τε οἱ πλεῖστοι κεχρημένοι. ἡ σοφὴ δὲ ἐκείνη τετρακτὺς ἐν τῷ κήπῳ μετὰ τῆς ἑταίρας ἔργοις ἐκύδαινον τὴν ἡδονήν. οὐκ ἂν οὖν ἐκφύγοιεν τὴν Βουζύγιον ἀρὰν ὅσοι μὴ δοκιμάζοντες σφίσι συμφέρειν τινὰ ἑτέροις ταῦτα παρακελεύονται ποιεῖν, ἢ αὖ τοὔμπαλιν. τοῦτο βραχέως ἡ γραφὴ δεδήλωκεν εἰρηκυῖα· ὃ μισεῖς, ἄλλῳ οὐ ποιήσεις. πλὴν οἱ γάμον δοκιμάζοντες ἡ φύσις ἡμᾶς ἐποίησεν φασὶν εὐθέτους πρὸς γάμον, ὡς δῆλον ἐκ τῆς σωμάτων κατασκευῆς τῶν τε ἀρρένων καὶ τῶν θηλειῶν, καὶ τὸ αὐξάνεσθε καὶ πληθύνεσθε συνεχῶς ἐπιβοῶνται. εἰ δὲ καὶ ταῦθ’ οὕτως ἔχει, ἀλλ’ αἰσχρόν γε αὐτοῖς δοκείτω καὶ τῶν ἀλόγων ζῴων τὸν ὑπὸ θεοῦ δημιουργηθέντα ἄνθρωπον ἀκρατέστερον εἶναι, ἃ τὴν ἐπιμιξίαν οὐ ποιεῖται πρὸς πολλὰ καὶ ἀνέδην, ἀλλὰ πρὸς ἓν καὶ ὁμόφυλον, οἷαι αἱ πελιάδες καὶ αἱ φάσσαι καὶ τὸ τρυγόνων γένος καὶ ὅσα τούτοις παραπλήσια. ἔτι, φασίν, ὁ ἄτεκνος τῆς κατὰ φύσιν τελειότητος ἀπολείπεται ἅτε μὴ ἀντικαταστήσας τῆ χώρᾳ τὸν οἰκεῖον διάδοχον· τέλειος γὰρ ὁ πεποιηκὼς ἐξ αὑτοῦ τὸν ὅμοιον, μᾶλλον δὲ ἐπειδὰν κἀκεῖνον τὸ αὐτὸ πεποιηκότα ἐπίδῃ, τουτέστιν ὅταν εἰς τὴν αὐτὴν καταστήσῃ φύσιν τὸ τεκνωθὲν τῷ τεκνώσαντι. Γαμητέον οὖν πάντως καὶ τῆς πατρίδος ἕνεκα καὶ τῆς τῶν παίδων διαδοχῆς καὶ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου τὸ ὅσον ἐφ’ ἡμῖν συντελειώσεως. ἐπεὶ καὶ γάμον τινὰ οἰκτείρουσιν οἱ ποιηταὶ ἡμιτελῆ καὶ ἄπαιδα, μακαρίζουσι δὲ τὸν ἀμφιθαλῆ. αἱ δὲ σωματικαὶ νόσοι μάλιστα τὸν γάμον ἀναγκαῖον δεικνύουσιν· ἡ γὰρ τῆς γυναικὸς κηδεμονία καὶ τῆς παραμονῆς ἡ ἐκτένεια τὰς ἐκ τῶν ἄλλων οἰκείων καὶ φίλων ἔοικεν ὑπερτίθεσθαι προσκαρτερήσεις, ὅσῳ τῇ συμπαθείᾳ διαφέρειν καὶ προσεδρεύειν μάλιστα πάντων προαιρεῖται, καὶ τῷ ὄντι κατὰ τὴν γραφὴν ἀναγκαία βοηθός. ὁ γοῦν κωμικὸς Μένανδρος καταδραμὼν τοῦ γάμου, ἀλλὰ καὶ τὰ χρήσιμα ἀντιτιθεὶς ἀποκρίνεται τῷ εἰπόντι πρὸς τὸ πρᾶγμα ἔχω κακῶς. Β.
pass_a_gloss: Since marriage seems to fall under pleasure and desire, it must be discussed. Marriage is therefore the first lawful union of a man and a woman for the sake of legitimate children. The comic poet Menander says, 'I give you my daughter to be your legitimate child, for the plow.' We are seeking whether one should marry, which is one of the things named according to its purpose. For to whom should one marry, and how should one marry, and what kind of person should one marry, and in what way? For one should not marry just anyone, nor at all times, but there is a time when it is fitting, and a person to whom it is fitting, and an age up to which it is fitting. Therefore, one should not marry just anyone, nor at all times, but neither should one marry completely without restraint, but rather to the one who is suitable, and in the way that is suitable, and at the time that is suitable, and for the sake of children, and in all things similarly, and not by force or necessity, but lovingly. From which Abraham says, concerning his wife, 'She is my sister,' as if she were his sister, 'for she is my sister, not by my mother, but by my father, and she became my wife,' teaching that those born of the same mother should not be taken in marriage. But let us briefly examine the story. Plato, in his external goods, ranks marriage, having provided for the immortality of our race and a kind of continuation, passed down from children to children. Democritus, on the other hand, rejects marriage and childbearing because of the many troubles and annoyances that come from them, which distract from more necessary things. Epicurus and those who place the good in pleasure and freedom from trouble and pain agree with him. According to the Stoics, marriage and childrearing are indifferent, but according to the Peripatetics, they are good. These people, having carried their doctrines to excess, have become slaves to pleasures. Some have used concubines, others have used courtesans, and most have used young men. The wise Theano, in her garden with her courtesan, used to rival her in deeds, not in pleasure. Therefore, those who do not test these things for themselves, but advise others to do them, or vice versa, would not escape the curse of Buzugius. The scripture has briefly shown this, saying, 'Do not do to another what you hate.' However, those who test marriage say that nature has made us straightforward for marriage, as is clear from the construction of our bodies, both male and female, and from the command to increase and multiply continuously. But if this is the case, it seems shameful to them that the human being, created by God, is more lacking in self-control than the irrational animals, which do not engage in intercourse with many or without restraint, but with one and with their own kind, such as doves and swallows and the species of birds. Furthermore, they say that the childless person lacks the perfection that comes from nature, since they have not replaced themselves with a successor; for one who has created a being like themselves is perfect, especially when they see that being create another being like themselves, that is, when they establish the one born in the same nature as the one who gave birth. Therefore, one should marry for the sake of the country, and for the sake of the succession of children, and for the completion of the world, insofar as it depends on us. For even the poets pity a marriage that is incomplete and childless, but they bless the one who has two children. Bodily illnesses also show that marriage is necessary; for the care of a wife and the attentiveness of a companion seem to surpass the attentiveness of other relatives and friends, inasmuch as they prefer to sympathize and attend to them more than all others, and according to the scripture, they are a necessary helper. The comic poet Menander, having run away from marriage, but also having set forth its useful aspects, responds to the one who says, 'I am doing badly in this matter.'

pass_b_english:
Since marriage appears to be driven by pleasure and desire, we must examine it. Marriage is, in fact, the first lawful union of a man and a woman for the sake of legitimate children. The comic poet Menander says, 'I give you my own daughter for the plow, that she may bear you legitimate children.' We are asking whether one ought to marry, a question that belongs among things named according to their purpose. For to whom should one marry, and in what condition, and what kind of woman, and in what state? One should not marry just anyone, nor at all times; there is a proper time, a proper person, and an age up to which it is fitting. Therefore, one should neither marry everyone at all times, nor marry completely without restraint, but rather the suitable person, in the suitable way, at the suitable time, for the sake of children, with complete similarity in all things, and not by force or necessity, but with love. Hence Abraham, speaking of his wife as if she were his sister, says, 'She is my sister, the daughter of my father but not of my mother, and she became my wife' (Leviticus 18:9), teaching that those born of the same mother should not be taken in marriage.

Let us now briefly review the history of thought on this. Plato ranks marriage among external goods, having secured the immortality of our race and a kind of continuity passed down like a torch from children to grandchildren. Democritus, on the other hand, rejects marriage and childbearing because of the many vexations and distractions they bring, which pull one away from more necessary matters. Epicurus and all who place the good in pleasure, freedom from trouble, and absence of pain agree with him. According to the Stoics, both marriage and childrearing are indifferent; according to the Peripatetics, they are good. These thinkers, having carried their doctrines to excess, became slaves to pleasures: some used concubines, others courtesans, and most used young men. The wise Theano, in her garden with her courtesan, rivaled her in deeds, not in pleasure. Therefore, those who do not test for themselves what benefits them, but command others to do these things—or the reverse—cannot escape the curse of Buzugius. Scripture has briefly indicated this, saying, 'Do not do to another what you hate.'

Yet those who approve of marriage argue that nature has made us well-suited for it, as is evident from the construction of our bodies, male and female, and from the continual command to 'increase and multiply' (Genesis 1:28). But if this is so, it should seem shameful to them that the human being, created by God, is more lacking in self-control than irrational animals, which do not mate with many or without restraint, but with one of their own kind—like doves, swallows, turtledoves, and similar species. Furthermore, they say the childless person falls short of natural perfection, having not replaced themselves with a successor in their place; for one who has produced a being like themselves is perfect, especially when they see that being do the same—that is, when the child born is established in the same nature as the parent.

Therefore, one must marry for the sake of one's country, for the succession of children, and for the completion of the world insofar as it depends on us. Even the poets pity a marriage that is incomplete and childless, but they bless the one who has children on both sides. Bodily illnesses also demonstrate that marriage is necessary; for the care of a wife and the devotion of her companionship seem to surpass the attentions of other relatives and friends, since she chooses to sympathize and attend more than anyone else, and according to Scripture she is a necessary helper. The comic poet Menander, though he fled from marriage, also sets forth its benefits, answering the one who says, 'I am doing badly in this matter.'
